old_value: In Savoie it makes light, low alcohol, lively dry whites meant to be drunk young.
final_value: In Savoie it makes low alcohol, lively dry whites meant to be drunk young.
reason: Trimmed "light": GuildSomm calls Jacquère medium bodied. Wine Folly: early drinking, low alcohol, lively dry wines. GuildSomm: good natural acidity, rarely above 12% alcohol, best within 3 years. Also Gilbert Gaillard (https://www.gilbertgaillard.com/en/magazine/discovery/savoy-jacquere-and-altesse-vie-for-a-lister-status): 11.5% ABV, drinks well within 2 to 3 years. Decanter Jefford link not used (not fetchable).

old_value: In Savoie it is fuller bodied than Jacquère, and Roussette de Savoie develops honeyed, nutty notes after a few years in bottle.
final_value: In Savoie it is fuller bodied than Jacquère, and Roussette de Savoie can show honeyed, nutty notes.
reason: Fuller body: GuildSomm ("fuller bodied wines than Jacquère") plus Gilbert Gaillard ("richer and riper white wine than Jacquère", https://www.gilbertgaillard.com/en/magazine/discovery/savoy-jacquere-and-altesse-vie-for-a-lister-status). Honey and nuts: GuildSomm (almond and honey) plus Wine Folly (honey, toast, nuts with age). Trimmed "after a few years in bottle": development with age is explicit only on Wine Folly.

old_value: In the dry whites here it adds weight and roundness, with exotic fruit and peach, balanced by fresh acidity.
reason: Only one grape specific source: Guide du Pays Basque (text credited to Irouléguy Distribution) says petit manseng brings volume, alcohol, exotic fruit, peach, acacia. INAO sheet (read from the PDF) describes Irouléguy whites in general (exotic fruit, balance of gras and acidity), not petit manseng. Hachette volume/roundness/peach comes from a single cuvée note (Lehia 2018), not a general statement.

old_value: From old, low yielding vines it gives deeply coloured, concentrated and quite tannic reds with brambly fruit, while young, high yielding vines give much thinner wine.
reason: Wine Society supports deeply coloured, quite tannic, brambly at its best and high yielding Carignan being of no interest, but says nothing about old vines or thin wine. Decanter "rise of Carignan" is premium and could not be read; Jancis Robinson pages return 403. No second independent Languedoc specific source confirmed.

old_value: As Muscat de Rivesaltes it makes a fortified sweet wine that stays notably fresh despite its sweetness.
reason: Hachette supports sweetness balanced by natural acidity and freshness. INAO sheet returns 403 (read only via search excerpts, not confirmed). Also Muscat de Rivesaltes is made from both Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat d'Alexandrie, so the appellation description is not specific to this grape.

old_value: Pineau de la Loire
reason: InterLoire map (PDF read): "CHENIN BLANC (also called Pineau de la Loire)". Wine Folly: "Sometimes referred to as Pineau de la Loire". Neither says it appears on labels; it is an alternative local name.

old_value: Here it has lively acidity, and the higher vineyards give leaner, livelier and longer lived wines.
reason: Trimmed the altitude claim: it rests only on the Decanter premium article (paywalled, not readable). Consortium: "belebende Säure". Decanter free feature (substituted for the premium one): "firm, reassuring acidity". Decanter free article says Pinot Bianco is moving to higher sites but does not say they give leaner, longer lived wines.

old_value: On thin soils of steep alpine terraces, Nebbiolo here is more perfumed and lighter bodied than in Barolo and Barbaresco, and wears its tannins more lightly.
final_value: Nebbiolo here is lighter bodied than in Barolo and wears its tannins more lightly.
reason: Decanter (Stephen Brook, quoting Nino Negri): thin soils, more perfumed, elegant and lighter bodied than Piedmont; wines wear their tannins lightly. Wine & Spirits (Stephanie Johnson, 2024, substituted for the unfetchable Wine Enthusiast page): lighter in tannin and more ethereal than the Langhe, less structure than Barolo. Trimmed perfume, thin soils, terraces and Barbaresco: single source.

old_value: Picked late, often in November, in hills where nights are cool, Taurasi Aglianico gains a savoury ripeness while keeping a fresh, almost saline acidity.
reason: Decanter buyer's guide is premium and could not be read. Wine Scholar Guild chart is vintage specific (November harvest only in 2021, diurnal range and acidity per vintage, mostly Campania/Irpinia wide), and does not mention savoury ripeness or saline acidity. No second source confirmed.

old_value: From old vines in high, stony vineyards it gives concentrated wines that keep their freshness and show a mineral trace.
reason: Appellation rules (PDF read in part): Calatayud Superior (Garnacha from vines over 50 years) has a deep aroma with mineral notes; the altitude, stony soil and concentration passages cited by the agent could not be located in the extracted text. Decanter is a single wine review (concentrated, plenty of freshness), not a regional statement. BBR gives 400 to 900 m but nothing on concentration, freshness or minerality.

old_value: In Cava it adds a fennel scent and a firm, fresh line of acidity to the blend.
final_value: In Cava it adds a fresh line of acidity to the blend.
reason: Trimmed fennel: only Decanter supports it (the Cava grapes piece is "In association with Cava DO", and the Jefford piece is the same publisher, single wine notes); Jeroboams is a merchant. Acidity: Wine Folly ("zingy acidity"; its Xarel-lo page: complements Macabeo with high acidity) and the DO sponsored Decanter piece ("low pH and fresh acidity"), which are different organisations. "Firm" dropped as not worded so in either.

old_value: In Jumilla it gives broad, fleshy reds with ripe fruit, generous alcohol and smooth, well integrated tannins.
reason: Decanter piece is labelled Sponsored and likely from the DO, so not independent of the appellation rules. MAPA appellation PDF could not be opened (certificate error) and per the agent describes Jumilla reds in general, not Monastrell. No independent second source found.

old_value: From old vines on the llicorella slate it gives intense wines with a stony, mineral character, while young vines here seldom give expressive wine.
final_value: From old vines it gives intense wines, while young vines here seldom give expressive wine.
reason: Decanter (Stephen Brook): century old vines are mostly Cariñena; old vine fruit has greater concentration; Cariñena needs at least 15 years before it can become expressive. Wine Folly: young Cariñena vineyards rarely produce high quality wine; old low yielding bush vines give intense wines. Trimmed llicorella minerality: both sources tie it to Priorat reds in general, not this grape.

old_value: On the llicorella slate it gives powerful, high alcohol wines that still keep a fresh acidity and a stony, mineral character.
reason: Only Decanter ties high alcohol (up to 15.5%) to Garnacha based wines, with enlivening acidity. Wine Folly gives high alcohol and "soft, moderate acidity" for Priorat reds in general, and minerality for the region, not the grape. The Decanter profile page is the same publisher (partner content). No second grape specific source.

old_value: Grown here since the 1950s and mostly blended with Verdejo, where it lightens the body and adds acidity.
final_value: Grown here since the 1950s, it lightens the body and adds acidity.
reason: DO Rueda: began to be grown in the 1950s; used for more lightness and a touch of acidity. SevenFifty Daily: grown since the 1950s; with Verdejo it lightens the body and boosts acidity. Trimmed "mostly blended with Verdejo": "mostly" is not stated by either.

old_value: Brought in during the region's revival in the 1970s, it is made on its own or blended with Verdejo.
final_value: It is made on its own or blended with Verdejo.
reason: Trimmed the 1970s and revival dating: 1970s only on SevenFifty, revival only on Decanter. Decanter (page labelled Sponsored): permitted as a single variety and blended with Verdejo. SevenFifty: blended with Verdejo; Rueda Sauvignon needs at least 85% Sauvignon Blanc. Decanter piece is sponsored, which is why only the plainly factual part is kept.

old_value: Here it gives fruit driven reds with well defined, ripe red fruit aromas.
final_value: Here it gives fruit driven reds with well defined, ripe red fruit aromas.
reason: Appellation rules (PDF read): red wine has "intensos aromas a frutos rojos maduros"; Valdeorras reds are labelled as such when at least 85% Mencía. Guía Peñín: reds mainly young Mencía with well defined fruity aromas, dry and fruity.

old_value: It is a little slimmer and firmer than Rheingau Riesling, with a fresh, hearty character.
reason: Rheingau comparison only on Falstaff ("schlanker und kerniger", said of Heppenheim and Bensheim). Weinbauverband "frisch, herzhaft" applies to the region's wines in general, not Riesling. No second source found.

old_value: A minor white grape in a valley given over mostly to Riesling, one of the Pinot varieties grown beside it.
final_value: One of the Pinot varieties grown here beside Riesling.
reason: DWI lists Weißburgunder among the main varieties beside Riesling; VDP: mainly Riesling but also Pinot family varieties; ProWein lists Pinot Blanc too. Removed "minor" (DWI names it a main variety) and "given over mostly to Riesling" (planting share).

old_value: The region's leading white grape, at its most distinctive on the red slate of the Roter Hang at Nierstein.
final_value: It is the main grape of the Roter Hang, the red slate slope at Nierstein.
reason: Rewritten from the supported part. ProWein: Riesling particularly multifaceted on the Roter Hang in Nierstein, primary in Pettenthal, Hipping and Ölberg. VDP Pettenthal site page (substituted): main variety Riesling, red clayey slate that gives the Roter Hang its name. Dropped "leading white grape" (ranking) and "most distinctive" (ProWein only). The DWI and VDP region pages cited do not link Riesling to the Roter Hang.

old_value: The cool nights of this northern region make it fresh, fine and mineral rather than broad.
reason: Only ProWein speaks of Pinot Blanc itself (fine fruit, minerality, freshness from one site, Freyburger Schweigenberg). DWI (cool nights, delicate crisp wines) and VDP (fresh, fragrant, filigreed) describe the region's wines in general.

old_value: One of the white Pinot varieties among the region's main grapes.
final_value: One of the white Pinot varieties among the region's main grapes.
reason: DWI lists Pinot Gris among the main varieties (Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir). Falstaff: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling and the white Pinot varieties top the variety statistics.

old_value: The swing between warm days and cool nights gives fresh, fine boned wines with intense aromas and a touch of minerality.
reason: Only ProWein speaks of Riesling (fresh, mineral wines from cool sites). DWI (day warmth and cool nights enhance aroma) and VDP (fresh, fragrant, filigreed, aromatic, intense) describe all the region's wines, not Riesling.

old_value: In the Alentejo it makes deeply coloured, dense and full bodied reds with firm tannins.
reason: Wine Folly supports intense colour, full body and firm tannins for Alentejo Alicante Bouschet. Decanter offers only the single word "dense" in an older article, and a further check (Decanter Alentejo panel, producer and single wine notes) found no second regional statement; tannins are described as soft and silky in some notes. Only one source supports the claim.

old_value: Mostly used with Grenache and Shiraz in the region's GSM blends.
final_value: Used with Grenache and Shiraz in the region's GSM blends.
reason: Wine Australia: Grenache often blended with Shiraz and Mataro (GSM). Wine Folly: a GSM blend contains Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro. Trimmed "Mostly": neither says it is mostly used that way.

old_value: The main white grape in this mostly red region.
reason: Both support Chardonnay among the main varieties of a red focused region, but "the main white grape" is a planting ranking excluded by the text rules, and nothing meaningful remains without it.

old_value: Crisp and juicy, with extra flesh on the middle palate from the maritime climate.
reason: No claim has two sources: Wine Australia says crisp, lively, juicy of the Semillon Sauvignon Blanc blends only; Halliday says maritime influence gives Sauvignon Blanc mid palate flesh but does not say crisp or juicy.

old_value: A long standing red here that takes a back seat to Cabernet Sauvignon.
final_value: A red that takes a back seat here to Cabernet Sauvignon.
reason: Halliday: Shiraz one of two best known reds, Cabernet "the king of Margaret River". Margaret River Wine Association: Cabernet among the most famous varieties, Shiraz the second red. The cited Wine Folly page (semillon-blend) does not mention Shiraz. Trimmed "long standing": only the Wine Association says it dates to the earliest days.

old_value: A blending partner for Cabernet Sauvignon in this mainly red region.
final_value: A blending partner for Cabernet Sauvignon here.
reason: Wine Australia: Cabernet sometimes blended with Merlot and Shiraz. Halliday: cabernet sometimes blended with merlot, shiraz. Trimmed "in this mainly red region": only Halliday.

old_value: Fresher and more savoury than warm climate Merlot, with black fruit, bright acidity and firm tannins.
reason: Wine Folly describes Long Island Bordeaux style blends in general, not Merlot; the Wine Enthusiast source is a single wine review. No regional Merlot specific second source.

old_value: Used with Chardonnay in the region's traditional method sparkling wines, as well as for some still red.
final_value: Used with Chardonnay in the region's traditional method sparkling wines.
reason: Wine Folly: traditional method sparkling with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Decanter (Lauren Mowery, substituted for the Wine Spectator single wine listing): Sparkling Pointe makes traditional method sparkling from Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay. Trimmed still red: only Decanter, about one winery, noting the climate usually does not suit it.

old_value: Grown in both El Dorado and Amador counties, on granite and volcanic hillside soils.
reason: El Dorado Winery Association covers El Dorado only; the Amador half and the Decanter source rest on a paywalled search snippet. Not two independent sources for the whole or a meaningful part (not re-fetched).

old_value: Usually big, ripe and richly textured, softer and more opulent than many Napa Cabernets.
reason: Only Wine Folly describes Paso Cabernet (big, bold, richly textured, opulent) and makes no Napa comparison. Wine Spectator "big, bold, ripe" is about San Juan Creek grapes generally. LCBO page returns 403.

old_value: Generous in texture yet kept fresh and lively by bright citrus acidity, which the valley's cool nights and fog help preserve.
reason: Winegrowers page says the diurnal shift preserves acidity in cool climate varieties but does not mention Chardonnay; the rest is single wine reviews and one producer. No second independent Chardonnay specific source.

old_value: From the highest coastal sites it is leaner and firmer, with an earthy edge and a dense core of acidity.
reason: No claim has two sources: Wine Spectator gives earthiness and a dense core of tannins and acidity for the highest sites; Wine Folly gives leaner Pinots with chalky minerality for Fort Ross Seaview; neither says firm.
